label: example_gace
title: Example
body_md:
\label{example_gace}

Suppose that $O=(L,A,Z',W',Y)$, where $A$ is a discrete or continuous treatment, $Y$ an outcome, and $L$ a vector of observed baseline covariates, and $Z'$ and $W'$ are correlates of an unmeasured confounder $U$, referred to as negative control treatments and negative control outcomes, respectively, satisfying $Z' \perp Y \mid A,L,U$ and  $(A,Z') \perp W' \mid L,U$. For each $a\in\mathcal{A}$, let $Y(a)$ denote the potential outcome under treatment level $a$ and $Y ( \cdot):= \left\{Y(a):a \in \mathcal{A} \right\}$. Let $O_{\text{full}}=(L,A,Z',W',Y, Y(\cdot))$. Let $P_0$ and $P_{\text{full},0}$ denote the unknown distributions of the factual random vector $O$ and the factual/counterfactual vector $O_{\text{full}}$. Suppose the goal is to estimate a parameter $\gamma(P_{\text{full},0}) := \mathbb{E}_{P_{\text{full},0}}\left\{ Y(A)\pi(A,L)\right\}$ where $\pi:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{L}\mapsto\mathbb{R}$ is a given specified weighting function. In particular, when $A$ is binary and $\pi(a,l) = 2a - 1$, $\gamma(P_{\text{full},0})$ is the average treatment effect (ATE), and when $\pi(a|l)=a$, $\gamma(P_{\text{full},0})=\mathbb{E}_{P_{full,0}}\{Y(1)\}$. Under the consistency assumption $Y(A)=Y$ and additional regularity conditions which essentially ensure that $Z'$ and $W'$ are strong proxies of the unmeasured confounder $U$, it can be shown (see \cite{miao2018identifying, tchetgen2020introduction, kallus2021causal, ghassami2022minimax, cui2024semiparametric}) that $\gamma(P_{\text{full},0})$ is identified and equal to $\theta(P_0)$ of the form~\eqref{eq:target_param}, with $W=(L,A,W')$, $Z=(L,A,Z')$, $
r(o) = 1$, $\tilde{m}(o;h) =\pi(a,l) \cdot h(w)$, $m(o;g) = y \cdot g(z)$
and corresponding Riesz representers $\tilde\rho_{P_0}(w) = \pi(a,l)/p_{0,A|L,W'}(a|l,w')$ and $\rho_{P_0}(z) = \mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left(Y \mid Z=z\right)$,
where $p_{0,A|L,W'}$ denotes the conditional density or probability mass function of $A$ given $(L,W')$. In this example $X:=(A,L)$. Note that while $\rho_{P_0}$ does not have structural zeros, $\tilde\rho_{P_0}$ will have exactly the same structural zeros as the weight function $\pi(a,l)$. For instance, if $A$ is binary and $\pi(a,l)=a$, then $\tilde\rho_{P_0}(w)=0$ for $w=(a=0,l,w')$.

label: example_mtp
title: Example
body_md:
\label{example_mtp} Suppose that under the same assumptions as in Example~\ref{example_gace}, with $A$ being continuous, we are interested in estimating the parameter $\gamma(P_{\text{full},0}) := \mathbb{E}_{P_{\text{full},0}}\left[ Y\{q(A)\}\right]$ where $q:\mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$ is a known function of the actually received treatment \citep{haneuse2013estimation, diaz2023nonparametric}. For instance, $q$ may take the form $q(a)=\left(a+\delta\right) I\{a\in[c,d-\delta-\varepsilon)\} +  \left\{a+\delta(d-a)/(\delta+\varepsilon)\right\} I\{a\in [d-\delta-\varepsilon, d]\}$ where  $[c,d]$ is the support of $A$ and $\delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are fixed pre-specified constants such that $d-\delta-\varepsilon >c$. \cite{olivas2025chap3} showed that under certain regularity conditions which include the requirement that $q$ be invertible and differentiable almost everywhere, $\theta(P_{full,0})$ is identified and admits the representation~\eqref{eq:target_param}, with
$ 
r(o) = 1$, $\tilde{m}(o;h) =h\{q(a),l,w'\}$, $m(o;g) = y \cdot g(z)$
and corresponding Riesz representers $\rho_{P_0}$ as in Example~\ref{example_gace}---since the map $m(o;g)$ is the same as in that example---and $\tilde\rho_{P_0}(w) = I\{a\in[c+\delta,d]\}\cdot\frac{dq^{-1}(a)}{da}\cdot\frac{p_{0,A|L,W}\{q^{-1}(a)\mid l,w'\}}{p_{0,A|L,W}(a|l,w')}$. Recalling that in this problem $X:=(L,A)$, we see that $\tilde\rho_{P_0}$ is zero outside the set $\{(l,a):a\in[c+\delta,d]\}$, so this last set plays the role of $\mathcal{X}_0$ for estimation of the solution of equation~\eqref{eq:int_eq_g}.

Suppose that $O=(\Delta,\Delta Y,X,Z')$, where $\Delta$ is binary, $Y$ is an outcome observed if and only if $\Delta = 1$, $X$ is a vector of covariates, and $Z'$ is a variable informative of $Y$, referred to as shadow variable, satisfying $Z'\perp \Delta\mid X,Y$ and $Z'\not\perp Y\mid X,\Delta=1$. Under certain structural assumptions on $\pi$,---namely, that $\pi(X,Y)$ depends only on features of $Y$ that are indirectly captured through $Z'$ given $X$---it can be shown \citep{miao2016varieties, li2023non,miao2024identification} that $\gamma(P_{\text{full},0})$ is identified and equals $\theta(P_0)$ of the form~\eqref{eq:target_param}, with $W=(X,\Delta Y)$, $Z=(X,Z')$,

body_md:

M_P(h)
&\stackrel{(i)}{=}4c^2 \max_{g\in \mathcal{G}} \mathbb{E}\left\{\rho(Z)g(Z)-I_0(X)r(O)h(W)g(Z)-c^2I_0(X)g(Z)^2\right\}
\\
&\stackrel{(ii)}{=}4c^2 \max_{g\in \mathcal{G}} \mathbb{E}\Big\{I_0(X)g(Z)\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)-c^2I_0(X)g(Z)^2\Big\}
\\
&=4c^2 \max_{g\in \mathcal{G}} \mathbb{E}\Big[I_0(X)g(Z)\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)-c^2I_0(X)g(Z)^2-\frac{1}{4c^2}I_0(X)\big\{\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]
\\
& \quad +\mathbb{E}\Big[I_0(X)\big\{\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]
\\
&=\max_{g\in \mathcal{G}} -\mathbb{E}\Big[I_0(X)\big\{2c^2g(Z)-\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]
+\mathbb{E}\Big[I_0(X)\big\{\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]
\\
&\stackrel{(iii)}{=}\mathbb{E}\Big[I_0(X)\big\{\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]
\end{align*}
where the equality $(i)$ holds because $\rho$ is the Riesz representer of the map $g \mapsto \mathbb{E}\left[m(O;g)\right]$, the equality $(ii)$ is because $I_0 h_{0}^\dag$ is a solution to equation~\eqref{eq:int_eq_h}, and the equality $(iii)$ is because by assumption, $(2c^2)^{-1}\cdot\mathcal{T}(h_0^\dag-h)\in\mathcal{G}$. Note that if $\mathcal{G}$ was unrestricted, part 1 would be, on expectation, the Frenchel conjugate representation of the squared function.
This concludes the proof of part 1.
To show part 2 write
\begin{align*}
\max_{g\in \mathcal{G}}& -\mathbb{E}\Big[I_0(X)\big\{2c^2g(Z)-\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]
+\mathbb{E}\Big[I_0(X)\big\{\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]\\
&\stackrel{(i)}{=}-\min_{g\in \mathcal{G}} \mathbb{E}\Big[\big\{I_0(X)g(Z)-I_0(X)\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]
+\mathbb{E}\Big[I_0(X)\big\{\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big)(Z)\big\}^2\Big]
\\
&\stackrel{(ii)}{=}-\big\Vert I_0\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big) - \mathcal{P}_{\overline{I_0\mathcal{G}}}\circ \mathcal{T}I_0(h_0^\dag-h)\big\Vert_2^2 + \big\Vert I_0\mathcal{T}\big(h_{0}^\dag-h\big) \big\Vert_2^2
\\
&\stackrel{(iii)}{=}\big\Vert  \mathcal{P}_{\overline{I_0\mathcal{G}}}\circ \mathcal{T}I_0(h_0^\dag-h)\big\Vert_2^2
\end{align*}
where the equality $(i)$ holds because $\mathcal{G}$ is a linear space, the equality $(ii)$ holds by the definition of the projection operator and the assumption that $\mathcal{P}_{\overline{I_0\mathcal{G}}}\circ \mathcal{T}I_0(h_0^\dag-h)
\in I_0\mathcal{G}$, and the equality $(iii)$ holds by Pythagorean Theorem. Hence, by Proposition~\ref{prop:sum_squares}, we have
$ 
M_P(h)=\Vert  \mathcal{P}_{\overline{I_0\mathcal{G}}}\circ \mathcal{T}I_0(h_0^\dag-h)\Vert_2^2=Q_\mathbb{J}(h)$. This concludes the proof of part 2.

   \mathcal{R}_n(I_0\cdot\mathcal{F},\:P,\:\delta) 
   &=\sum_{m=1}^n \mathbb{E}_{P,P_\varepsilon}\Big\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_0(\delta)}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_iI_0(X_i)f(O_i)\Big\vert N=m\Big\}P(N=m)\\
     &=\sum_{m=1}^n \mathbb{E}_{P,P_\varepsilon}\Big\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_0(\delta)}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_if(O_i)\Big\vert X_i\in\mathcal{X}_0,\forall \:i=1,\dots,m\Big\}\frac{m}{n}P(N=m)\\
     &=\sum_{m=1}^n \mathbb{E}_{Q,P_\varepsilon}\Big\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_0(\delta)}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_if(O_i)\Big\}\frac{m}{n}P(N=m)\\
      &=\sum_{m=1}^n \mathcal{R}_m(\mathcal{F},Q,\:\delta/\sqrt{\mu_0})\:\frac{m}{n}\:P(N=m)=\mathbb{E}\left\{\mathcal{R}_N(\mathcal{F},Q,s)\frac{N}{n}\right\},
\end{align*}
where the second equality follows because the $O_1,\dots,O_n$ are i.i.d.

Let $\mathcal{D}_n$ be the event $\{N-n\mu_0<-n\mu_0/2\}$. By Hoeffding inequality we have $P(D_n)<\exp\{-2n^2\mu_0^2/(4n)\}=\exp(-dn)$ where $d:=\mu_0^2/2$. 
Then for $s:=\sup\{\delta_m: n\mu_0/2\le m\le n\}$
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{R}_n(I_0\cdot\mathcal{F},P,\delta)&=\mathbb{E}\left\{\mathcal{R}_N(\mathcal{F},Q,s)\frac{N}{n}I_{\mathcal{D}_N}(N)\right\}+E\left\{\mathcal{R}_N(\mathcal{F},Q,s)\frac{N}{n}I_{\mathcal{D}_N^c}(N)\right\}\\
    &\le bP(\mathcal{D}_n)+\sup_{n\mu_0/2\le m\le n}\mathcal{R}_m(\mathcal{F},Q,s)\\
    &\le b\exp(-dn)+s^2.
\end{align*}
Let $\varepsilon$ be such that $1/\mu_0>1+\varepsilon^2$. Because by assumption $\delta_n^2=o(\exp\{-dn\})$, then there exists $n_0$ such that if $n\ge n_0$, $b\exp(-dn)\le\varepsilon^2s^2$. On the other hand, our choice of $\varepsilon$ implies that  $\mathcal{R}_n(I_0\cdot\mathcal{F},P,\delta)>\mathcal{R}_n(I_0\cdot\mathcal{F},P,s\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2})$. Then, the last display implies that $\mathcal{R}_n(I_0\cdot\mathcal{F},P,s\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2})<(1+\varepsilon^2)s^2$. Therefore, $\delta_n'\le s\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}=O(\alpha_{\lfloor n\mu_0/2\rfloor})$ by the assumed monotonicity of $\alpha_n$.

We denote the support of random variables $(V_1,\dots,V_k)$ and their conditional versions $V_1|(V_2=v_2,\dots,V_k=v_k)$, for $k\ge2$, as $\text{supp}(V_1,\dots,V_k)$ and $\text{supp}(V_1|V_2=v_2,\dots,V_k=v_k)$.

 Observe that $q$, defined in Example~\ref{example_mtp}, is strictly monotone and differentiable a.e. with respect to $P_{0,A}$, and admits an inverse that is differentiable a.e. with positive derivative.

Suppose that $\tilde\rho_{P_0}(a,l,w) = I_0(a,l)\cdot\frac{dq^{-1}(a)}{da}\cdot\frac{p_{0,A|L,W}\{q^{-1}(a)\mid l,w\}}{p_{0,A|L,W}(a|l,w)}$, where $I_0(a,l):=I\{a\in[c+\delta,d]\}$, is bounded by some $B_0>0$. Then, for any $h\in\mathcal{L}^2(A,L,W)$,
\begin{align*}
    \Vert\widetilde{m}(O;h)\Vert_2^2&=\iint \left[\int h\{q(a),l,w\}^2p_{0,A|L,W}(a|l,w)da\right]dP_0(l,w)\\
    &\stackrel{(i)}{=}\iiint h(\tilde a,l,w)^2\cdot I\{\tilde a\in[c+\delta,d]\}\cdot \frac{dq^{-1}(\tilde a)}{d\tilde a}p_{0,A|L,W}(q^{-1}(\tilde a)|l,w)\:d\tilde a\cdot dP_{0}(l,w)\\
    &\stackrel{(ii)}{=}\iiint h(\tilde a,l,w)^2\cdot I_0(\tilde a,l)\cdot\tilde \rho_{P_0}(\tilde a,l,w)p_{0,A|L,W}(\tilde a|l,w)\:d\tilde a\cdot dP_{0}(l,w)\\
    &\stackrel{(iii)}{\le} B_0\iiint I_0(\tilde a,l)\cdot h(\tilde a,l,w)^2p_{0,A|L,W}(\tilde a|l,w)\:d\tilde a\cdot dP_0(l,w)=B_0\cdot \Vert I_0h\Vert_2^2,
\end{align*}
    where the equality in (i) follows from the change of variable $\tilde a = q(a)$, which is valid since $q$ has an a.e. differentiable inverse with strictly positive derivative and maps $[c,d]$ onto $[c+\delta,d]$. Equality (ii) follows directly from the definition of $\tilde\rho_{P_0}$, and the inequality (iii) uses the assumption that $|\tilde\rho_{P_0}(a,l,w)|\le B_0$ for all $(a,l,w)\in\text{supp}(A,L,W)$. This proves the first inequality in part 1 of Assumption~\ref{ass:bounded} with constant $B_2=\sqrt{B_0}$.

    To verify part 2 of Assumption~\ref{ass:bounded}, we impose the following \textit{common support} assumption: $ \text{supp}(A|L=l,U=u)=\text{supp}(A|L=l)$ for all $(l,u)\in\text{supp}(L,U)$, which is standard in proximal inference (see \cite{olivas2025chap3}). This assumption, together with the fact that $W$ is a negative control outcome-- i.e., $(A,Z)\perp W|L,U$ -- imply that $\text{supp}(A|L=l,W=w)=\text{supp}(A|L=l)$ for all $(l,w)\in\text{supp}(L,W)$. Moreover, $\text{supp}(A,L,W)=[c,d]\times\text{supp}(L,W)$ given that $\text{supp}(A|L=l)=[c,d]$ for all $l\in\mathcal{L}$.
    
    Next, we define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal{H}$ as follows: $ h\leftrightarrow h'$ if and only if $h(a,l,w)=h'(a,l,w)$ for all $ (a,l,w)\in[c+\delta, d]\times\text{supp}(L,W)$. Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}:=\{[h]:h\in\mathcal{H}\}$ denote the set of equivalences classes in $\mathcal{H}$ under this relation. Note that $h\leftrightarrow h'$ iff $h-h'\in[0]:=\{h\in\mathcal{H}:h(a,l,w)=0\:\forall (a,l,w)\in[c+\delta,d]\times\text{supp}(L,W)\}$. In the special case of a Gaussian RKHS, the zero function is the only function that vanishes on a non-empty open subset (see Corollary 4.44 of \cite{steinwart2008support}); hence each equivalence class contains a single function, and $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$ coincides with $\mathcal{H}$. Define the map $\tilde d:\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}\times\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}\mapsto\mathbb{R}$ by
    \[
    \tilde d([h_1],[h_2]):=\inf\{\Vert h_1-h_2+v\Vert_\mathcal{H}\mid v\in[0]\}.
    \]
    Note that $\tilde d$ is well-defined because the set in the right hand side is invariant to the choice of representer $h_1\in[h_1]$ and $h_2\in[h_2]$.
    We now verify that $\tilde d$ is a metric on $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$. By construction, $\tilde d$ is symmetric. To see that the triangle inequality holds, given $\epsilon >0$ and $[h_1],[h_2],[h_3]\in\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$, pick $v,v'\in[0]$ such that $\Vert h_1-h_2+v\Vert_\mathcal{H} < \tilde d([h_1],[h_2]) + \epsilon$ and $\Vert h_2-h_3+v'\Vert_\mathcal{H} < \tilde d([h_2],[h_3]) + \epsilon$. Then, $\Vert h_1-h_3+v+v'\Vert_\mathcal{H} \le \tilde d([h_1],[h_2])+d([h_2],[h_3])+ 2 \epsilon$. Because $v+v'\in[0]$, it follows that $\tilde d([h_1],[h_3]) \le \tilde d([h_1],[h_2])+\tilde d([h_2],[h_3]) + 2 \epsilon$. Since this holds for all $\epsilon >0$, the triangular inequality follows.

    Finally, we show that $\tilde d([h_1],[h_2])=0$ if and only if $[h_1]=[h_2]$. The if direction is trivial since $\tilde d([h],[h])=\inf\{\Vert v\Vert\mid v\in[0]\}=0$ for all $[h]\in\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$. To show the only if direction suppose that $\tilde d([h_1],[h_2])=0$ but $[h_1]\neq[h_2]$. Then there exist representatives $h_1\in[h_1]$, $h_2\in[h_2]$, and a point $(a_0,l_0,w_0)\in[c+\delta,d]\times\text{supp}(L,W)$ such that $ h_1(a_0,l_0,w_0)\neq h_2(a_0,l_0,w_0)$. Let $\epsilon:=|h_1(a_0,l_0,w_0)- h_2(a_0,l_0,w_0)|>0$, and $ k:=[\sup_{(a,l,w)\in\text{supp}(A,L,W)}K_{\mathcal{H}}\{(a,l,w),(a,l,w)\}]^{1/2}<\infty$. By the definition of $\tilde d$ and the fact that $\tilde d([h_1],[h_2])=0$, there exists $v'\in[0]$ such that $\Vert h_1-h_2+v'\Vert_\mathcal{H}<\epsilon/k$. Let $h_1':=h_1+v'$. Then we arrive at the following contradiction:
 \begin{align*}
        k\Vert h_1'-h_2\Vert_\mathcal{H}<|h_1(a_0,l_0,w_0)-h_2(a_0,l_0,w_0)|=|h'_1(a_0,l_0,w_0)-h_2(a_0,l_0,w_0)|\le k\Vert h_1'-h_2\Vert_\mathcal{H},
    \end{align*}
 where the equality holds because $h_1\leftrightarrow h'_1$ and the final inequality because for any $h\in\mathcal{H}$, $\Vert h\Vert_\infty\le k\:\Vert h\Vert_\mathcal{H}$. Hence, $\tilde d([h_1],[h_2])=0$ implies $[h_1]=[h_2]$.

 We now show that $(\widetilde{\mathcal{H}},d)$ is separable. Since $K_\mathcal{H}$ is continuous and $\text{supp}(A,L,W)$ is compact, $\mathcal{H}$ is separable under the metric induced by its norm (see Proposition 11.7 of \cite{paulsen2016introduction}). Let $\{h_n\}\subset\mathcal{H}$ be a countable dense subset, and consider the set of equivalence classes $\{[h_n]\}$. We claim this set is dense in $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$. Indeed, for any $[h]\in\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$ and $\epsilon>0$, there exists a representative $h'\in[h]$ and some $h_n\in\mathcal{H}$ such that $\Vert h'-h_n\Vert_\mathcal{H}<\epsilon$. Then $d([h],[h_n])\le\Vert h-h_n\Vert_\mathcal{H}<\epsilon$, so $\{[h_n]\}$ is dense in $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$, and thus $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$ is separable.

    Next, consider the class $\widetilde{m}\circ \mathcal{H}:=\{o\mapsto h(q(a),l,w)\}$, which is in a one-to-one correspondence with $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$. More precisely, the map $h\mapsto \widetilde{m}(\cdot,h)$ is well-defined on equivalence classes, since $ \widetilde{m}(o;h_1)=\widetilde{m}(o;h_2)$ for all $o\in\mathcal{O}$ iff $h_1(q(a),l,w)=h_1(q(a),l,w)$ for all $(a,l,w)\in[c,d]\times\text{supp}(L,W)$, $h_1(a,l,w)=h_2(a,l,w)$ for all $(a,l,w)\in[c+\delta,d]\times\text{supp}(L,W)$ (since $q
    \left([c,d]\right)=[c+\delta,d]$) iff  $h_1\leftrightarrow h_2$. Thus, we can equip $\widetilde{m}\circ\mathcal{G}$ with the metric $d$ defined as:
    \[
    d(f_1,f_2):=\tilde d([h_{f_1}],[h_{f_2}])\quad \text{ for any }f_1,f_2\in\widetilde{\mathcal{H}},
    \]
    where $[h_{f_1}]$ and $[h_{f_2}]$ are their corresponding equivalence classes in $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$. This
    yields $(\widetilde{m}\circ\mathcal{H},d)$ a separable metric space. By construction, the metric $d$ is controlled by the RKHS norm.

    Finally, we show that the metric $d$ dominates the sup-norm on $\widetilde{m}\circ\mathcal{H}$. For any $f_1,f_2\in \widetilde{m}\circ\mathcal{H}$, let $[h_{f_1}]$ and $[h_{f_2}]$ be their corresponding equivalence classes, and take any representatives $h_{f_1}\in [h_{f_1}]$ and $h_{f_2}\in [h_{f_2}]$. Then, for any $o\in\mathcal{O}$, we have
    \begin{align*}
        |f_1(o)-f_2(o)|:=|\widetilde{m}(o;h_{f_1})-\widetilde{m}(o;h_{f_2})|&=|h_{f_1}(q(a),l,w)-h_{f_2}(a,l,w)|\le k\Vert h_{f_1}-h_{f_2}\Vert_\mathcal{H}.
    \end{align*}
    Since the representatives were arbitrary, we conclude that $ \sup_{o\in\mathcal{O}} |f_1(o)-f_2(o)|\le k\cdot \tilde d([h_1],[h_2])=k\cdot d(f_1,f_2)$, implying that $d$ dominates the metric induced by the sup-norm with constant $B_3=k$. This completes the verification of part 2 of Assumption~\ref{ass:bounded}.

Let $P_0^q:=P_0\circ q^{-1}$ be the pushforward measure of $P_0$ under $q$. For any $g\in\mathcal{G}_{B_1}$, the composition $m(\:\cdot\:,g)=g\circ q(\cdot)$ satisfies
\[
\Vert m(\:\cdot\:,g)\Vert_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_0)}^2=\Vert g\circ q \Vert_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_0)}^2=\int_\mathcal{Z}g\{q(z)\}^2dP_0(z)=\int_{q(\mathcal{Z})}g(\tilde z)^2d(P_0\circ q^{-1})(\tilde z)=\Vert g\Vert_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_0^q)}^2,
\]
so the map $g\mapsto g\circ q=m(\:\cdot\:,g)$ is an isometry between $(\mathcal{G}_{B_1},\mathcal{L}^2(P_0^q))$ and $(m\circ\mathcal{G}_{B_1},\mathcal{L}^2(P_0))$.

Observe that the Rademacher complexity is preserved under reparameterization: if  $Z_1,\dots,Z_n\sim P_{0}$, $\tilde Z_1,\dots,\tilde Z_n\sim P_0^q$, and $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n$ are i.i.d. Rademacher variables, then $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_ig\{q(Z_i)\}^2=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_ig(\tilde Z_i)^2$,
so for all $\delta>0$, $\mathcal{R}_n(m\circ \mathcal{G}_{B_1},\:P_0,\:\delta) = \mathcal{R}_n(\mathcal{G}_{B_1},\:P_0^q,\:\delta)$. Then the critical radius of $m\circ\mathcal{G}_{B_1}$ under $P_0$ equals the critical radius of $\mathcal{G}_{B_1}$ under $P_0^q$. The result follows because the critical radius of an RKHS class is preserved up to multiplicative constants under changes of measure. That $o \mapsto m(o, g) = g(q(z))$ is star shaped follows because $o \mapsto m(o, g) = g(q(z))$ is linear in $g$ and $\mathcal{G}_{B_1}$ is star-shaped.

title: Proof
body_md:
Linearity is immediate from that of $I_0^{op}$, $\mathcal{T}$, and $T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}$. Boundedness of $I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}\mid_\mathcal{H}$ follows because for $h \in \mathcal{H}$, it holds that $\Vert I_0^{op}\mathcal{T}h\Vert_2^2\le\Vert r\Vert_\infty^2\Vert h\Vert_2^2\le\Vert r\Vert_\infty^2\Vert h\Vert_\infty^2\le k_1^2\Vert r\Vert_\infty^2\Vert h\Vert_\mathcal{H}^2$,
   where $k_1^2=\sup_{w\in\mathcal{W}}K_\mathcal{H}(w,w)<\infty$. Boundedness of $I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}\circ T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}$ follows because $T_\mathcal H^{1/2}$(by Lemma~\ref{lemma:null_space}(f)), $\mathcal T$, and $I_0^{op}$ are all bounded, and so is their composition.

   To determine the adjoint of $I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}\mid_\mathcal{H}$, let $h\in\mathcal{H}$ and $g\in\mathcal{L}^2(P_Z)$. Then, applying Lemma~\ref{lemma:null_space}(g) yields $\langle I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}h,g\rangle_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_Z)}=\langle \mathcal{T}h,I_0^{op}g\rangle_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_Z)}=\left\langle h,\mathcal{T}^*\circ I_0^{op}g\right\rangle_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_W)}=\left\langle h,T_\mathcal{H}\circ\mathcal{T}^*\circ I_0^{op}g\right\rangle_\mathcal{H}$. Hence, $(I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}\mid_\mathcal{H})^*=T_\mathcal{H}\circ\mathcal{T}^*\circ I_0^{op}$. Now let $h\in\mathcal{L}^2(P_W)$ and $g\in\mathcal{L}^2(P_Z)$. Since $T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}$ is self-adjoint, we have $ \langle I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}\circ T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}h,g\rangle_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_Z)}=\langle T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}h,\mathcal{T}^*\circ I_0^{op}g\rangle_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_W)}=\langle h,T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}\circ\mathcal{T}^*\circ I_0^{op}g\rangle_{\mathcal{L}^2(P_W)}$. Thus $(I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}\circ T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2})^*=T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}\circ\mathcal{T}^*\circ I_0^{op}$.

body_md:
To simplify notation, we drop the subscripts $KRAS$ from $h_{0,KRAS}^\dag$ and $h'_{0,KRAS}$. Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:relizability}--\ref{ass:K_H}, $h_0^\dag$ in~\eqref{def:h_0_dag} is well-defined, and $\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}$ is bounded (see Section~\ref{sec:conv_analysis}). 

By Lemma~\ref{lemma:null_space} (e), there exists a unique $h_0'\in\mathcal{N}(T_\mathcal{H})^\perp$ such that $h_0^\dag=T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}h_0'$. Since $\rho=\mathcal{T}\left(I_0h_0^\dag\right)=I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}h_0^\dag=I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}\circ T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}h_0'=\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}h_0'$
it follows that $h_0'$ solves equation~\eqref{eq:rkhs_int_eq_h}. It remains to show that it is the solution of minimal $\mathcal{L}^2(P_{W})-$norm. Let $h_1\in\mathcal{L}^2(P_{W})$ be any solution to~\eqref{eq:rkhs_int_eq_h}. Decompose $h_1$ as $h_1'+h_1^\perp$, where $h_1'\in\mathcal{N}(T_\mathcal{H})$ and $h_1^\perp\in\mathcal{N}(T_\mathcal{H})^\perp$. Since $\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}h_1^\perp =\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}h_1$, it follows that $h_1^\perp$ also solves equation~\eqref{eq:rkhs_int_eq_h}. Moreover, $\rho=\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}h_1^\perp=I_0^{op}\circ\mathcal{T}\circ T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}h_1^\perp =\mathcal{T}(I_0T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}h_1^\perp)$, so $T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}h_1^\perp\in\mathcal{H}_0$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:null_space} (d), $T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}$ restricted to $\mathcal{N}(T_\mathcal{H})^\perp$ is an isometry, so $\Vert h_1^\perp\Vert_2=\Vert T^{1/2}_\mathcal{H}h_1^\perp\Vert_\mathcal{H}\ge \Vert h_0^\dag\Vert_\mathcal{H}^2=\Vert h_0'\Vert_2^2$ with equality iff $T^{1/2}_{\mathcal{H}}h_1^\perp=h_0^\dag=T_\mathcal{H}^{1/2}h_0'$, which by Lemma~\ref{lemma:null_space} (e) implies $h_1^\perp=h_0'$. Therefore, $\Vert h_1\Vert_2^2=\Vert h_1'\Vert_2^2+\Vert h_1^\perp\Vert_2^2\ge \Vert h_0'\Vert_2^2$, with equality, i.e., $\Vert h_1\Vert_2=\Vert h_0'\Vert_2$, if and only if $h_1'=0$ and $h_1^\perp=h_0'$. This shows that $h_0'$ is the unique solution to equation~\eqref{eq:rkhs_int_eq_h} of minimal $\mathcal{L}^2(P_{W})$-norm.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\underset{\sim}{o}:=(o_1,\dots, o_n)\in\mathcal{O}^n$ and define $g(\underset{\sim}{o};f):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nt_f(o_i)$, $A_1(\underset{\sim}{o}):=\sup_{f\in \mathcal{F}} g(\underset{\sim}{o};f)$, and $A_2(\underset{\sim}{o}):=\sup_{f\in \mathcal{S}}g(\underset{\sim}{o};f)$. We will show that $A_1(\underset{\sim}{o})=A_2(\underset{\sim}{o})$.  

Clearly $A_2(\underset{\sim}{o})\le A_1(\underset{\sim}{o})$ because $\mathcal{S}\subset \mathcal{F}$. Suppose that $A_2(\underset{\sim}{o})<A_1(\underset{\sim}{o})$ and set $\varepsilon:=A_1(\underset{\sim}{o})-A_2(\underset{\sim}{o})>0$. By the definition of the supremum, there exists $f_\varepsilon\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $A_1(\underset{\sim}{o})-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}< g(\underset{\sim}{o};f_{\varepsilon})$.
Now, the map $f\mapsto g(\underset{\sim}{o};f)$ is continuous because the map $f\mapsto t_f(o_i)$ is continuous for each $i$. Then, there exists $\delta>0$ such that $d(f,f_\varepsilon)<\delta$ implies $|g(\underset{\sim}{o};f)-g(\underset{\sim}{o};f_{\varepsilon})|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$. Since $\mathcal{S}$ is dense in $\mathcal{F}$, there exits $f_s\in \mathcal{S}$ such that $d(f_s,f_\varepsilon)<\delta$. Then, $g(\underset{\sim}{o};f_s)>g(\underset{\sim}{o};f_{\varepsilon})-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}>A_1(\underset{\sim}{o})-\varepsilon=A_2(\underset{\sim}{o})$, which contradicts the definition of $A_2(\underset{\sim}{o})$. We thus conclude that $A_1(\underset{\sim}{o})=A_2(\underset{\sim}{o})$.

Next, since $g(\cdot;f):\mathcal{O}^n\mapsto\mathbb{R}$ is measurable for all $f\in \mathcal{S}$, and the map $f\mapsto g(\underset{\sim}{o};f)$ is continuous for all $\underset{\sim}{o}\in\mathcal{O}^n$, Lemma A.3.17 of \cite{steinwart2008support} ensures that the mapping $(\underset{\sim}{o},f)\mapsto g(\underset{\sim}{o};f)$ is measurable on $\mathcal{O}^n\times\mathcal{S}$. Then, the map $\underset{\sim}{o}\mapsto\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}}g(\underset{\sim}{o};f)$ is also measurable because $\mathcal{S}$ is countable. Hence, $\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}}g(O_1,\dots,O_n;f)= \sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}g(O_1,\dots,O_n;f)$
is a well-defined random variable. This completes the proof.

body_md:
Suppose that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The assumptions of Corollary \ref{corollary:countable_Lf} hold with $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying: (1.1) $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly bounded by $b$, (1.2) for each $o\in\mathcal{O}$, the evaluation functional $f\mapsto f(o)$ is continuous relative to $d$, and (1.3) $f=0$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}$.
    \item $t_f$ satisfies $t_f=0$ when $f=0$.
    \item There exists a constant $L$ such that for any $f_1,f_2\in\mathcal{L}^2(P_O)$, $|t_{f_1}(o)-t_{f_2}(o)|\le L\cdot\left\vert f_1(o)-f_2(o)\right\vert$ for all $o\in\mathcal{O}$ ($o\in\mathcal{O}_0$).
\end{enumerate}
Define $h_f$ as in Corollary \ref{corollary:countable_Lf} with $\beta = 1$. For any $r>0$ define $\mathcal{F}_r:=\left\{f \in \mathcal{F}\::\:\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\Vert_2 \le r \right\}$ and $Z_n(r):=\sup_{f\in \mathcal{F}_r} \big\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nh_f(O_i) \big\vert$. Then, $Z_n(r)$ is a well-defined random variable and for all $u>0$, $\text{P}\left\{Z_n(r)\ge 4L\mathcal{R}_n\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}, r\right)+u\right\}\le 2\exp\Big(-\frac{nu^2}{8eL^2r^2+128ebL^2\mathcal{R}_n\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot \mathcal{F},r\right)+8bLu}\Big)$,
    where $e=\exp(1)$ and $\mathcal{R}_n(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F},r)$ is the localized Rademacher complexity of radius $r$ of the function class $I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}:=\{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\:|\:f\in\mathcal{F}\}$.
    Moreover, if $\delta_n$ is any solution to the inequality $\mathcal{R}_n\left(star\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}\right),\delta\right)\le\frac{\delta^2}{b}$,
    then for each $r\ge\delta_n$, $ \text{P}\{Z_n(r)\ge\frac{4Lr\delta_n}{b}+u\}\le 2\exp\Big(-\frac{nu^2}{8eL^2r^2+128eL^2r\delta_n+8bLu}\Big)$.
    \label{lemma:lemma11foster}

title: Proof
body_md:
By assumption 1, the conclusion of Corollary \ref{corollary:countable_Lf} holds; i.e., $Z_n(r)$ is well-defined. Furthermore, $ Z_n(r)=\sup_{f\in \mathcal{S}_r} \big\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nh_f(O_i) \big\vert$.
where $\mathcal{S}_r := \mathcal{S} \cap \mathcal{F}_r$.
Now define the function class $\mathcal{C}:=\left\{\alpha h_f\::\:\alpha\in\{-1,1\}, f\in\mathcal{S}_r\right\}$ which is countable by construction. With $\mathcal{C}$ so defined we have that $ Z_n(r)=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{C}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nh(O_i)$.

For any $h\in\mathcal{C}$, write $h=\alpha h_f$ for some $\alpha\in\{-1,1\}$ and $f\in\mathcal{S}_r$. Letting $f'=0$, we have
\begin{align*}
    |h(o)|&\le |t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(o)|+\mathbb{E}\big\{\big\vert t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O)\big\vert\big\}\\
    &=|t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(o)-t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f'}(o)|+\mathbb{E}\big\{\big\vert t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O)-t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f'}(O)\big\vert\big\}\\
    &\le L\cdot I_{\mathcal{O}_0}(o)\big\vert f(o)-f'(o)\big\vert + L\cdot \mathbb{E}\big\{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}(O)\big\vert f(O)-f'(O)\big\vert \big\}\le 2Lb,
\end{align*}
where the first inequality is by the triangle inequality, the first and second equalities are by assumptions 1.3 and 2, the second inequality is by assumption 3, and the third inequality is by assumption 1.1. We thus conclude that $\mathcal{C}$ is uniformly bounded by $2Lb$. Since $\mathcal{C}$ is countable, applying Talagrand inequality (Lemma \ref{lemma:talagrand}) we obtain that, for any $u>0$,
    \[
    \text{P}\left[Z_n(r)\ge \mathbb{E}\left\{Z_n(r)\right\}+u\right]\le 2\exp\left(-\frac{nu^2}{8e\sup_{h\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{E}[h(O)^2]+32ebL\mathbb{E}\left\{Z_n(r)\right\}+8bLu}\right).
    \]
    Again, take $h\in\mathcal{C}$ and write $h=\alpha h_f$ for some $\alpha\in\{-1,1\}$ and $f\in\mathcal{S}_r$. Thus $\mathbb{E}[h(O)^2]=\text{var}[t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O)]\le \mathbb{E}[\{ t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O)\}^2]\le L^2\mathbb{E}[\{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}(O)\cdot f(O)\}^2]\le L^2r^2$, where the second inequality follows by invoking assumption 3 applied to $f_1=I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f$ and $f_2=0$ and noting that by assumption 2, $t_{f_2}=0$, and the third inequality is because $f\in\mathcal{F}_r$.

   We now bound $\mathbb{E}\{Z_n(r)\}=\mathbb{E}\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n[t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i)-\mathbb{E}\{t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O)\}]\vert\}$ using a symmetrization argument. Letting $\{O'_i\}_{i=1}^n$ be independent copies of $O$ and independent of $\{O_i\}_{i=1}^n$, we can write $\mathbb{E}\{Z_n(r)\}=\mathbb{E}\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_r}\vert\mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\{t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i)-t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i')\}]\vert\}$. By the inequality $\sup_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}\left\{|d(O)|\right\}\le\mathbb{E}\left\{\sup_{d\in\mathcal{D}}|d(O)|\right\}$, which is valid for any countable class $\mathcal{D}$ of real-valued measurable functions, we conclude $\mathbb{E}\{Z_n(r)\}\le\mathbb{E}[\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\{t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i)-t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i')\}\vert]$.

    Now, let $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n$ be $n$ i.i.d. Rademacher random variables, independent of $O_i$ and $O'_i$ for all $i=1,\dots,n$. Given this independence assumption, for any function $f\in\mathcal{F}$, the $n \times 1$ random vector with $i^{th}$ component $\varepsilon_i\{t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i)-t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i')\}$ has the same joint distribution as the $n \times 1$ random vector with $i^{th}$ component $ t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i)-t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i')$.
    Hence, $\mathbb{E}[\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i\{t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i)-t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i')\}\vert]\le2\mathbb{E}\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}(O_i)\vert\}\\=2\mathbb{E}\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}'_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i  t_f(O_i)\vert\}$.
where $\mathcal{S}_r':=\left\{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f:f\in\mathcal{S}_r\right\}$. Next, invoking the Ledoux-Talagrand contraction inequality (see inequality (5.61) of \cite{wainwright2019high}), we obtain $ 2\mathbb{E}\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}'_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i  t_f(O_i)\vert\}\le
4L\mathbb{E}\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}'_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i f(O_i)\vert\}\\=4L\mathbb{E}\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i I_{\mathcal{O}_0}(O_i)\cdot f(O_i)\vert\}=4L\mathbb{E}\{\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_r}\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i I_{\mathcal{O}_0}(O_i)\cdot f(O_i)\vert\}=4L \mathcal{R}_n\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F},r\right)$
    where the second equality follows by applying Corollary \ref{corollary:countable_Lf} to the functions $t_f(o,\varepsilon):=\varepsilon f(o)$ and $\beta=0$, noting that assumption 3 of the corollary holds because the map $f\mapsto f(o)$ is continuous (assumption 1.2). Thus, $\mathbb{E}\left\{Z_n(r)\right\}\le4L\cdot \mathcal{R}_n\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F},r\right)$. Therefore, $ \text{P}[Z_n(r)\ge 4L\cdot \mathcal{R}_n(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F},r)+u]\le \text{P}[Z_n(r)\ge \mathbb{E}\{Z_n(r)\}+u]\\ \le2\exp\Big(-\frac{nu^2}{8eL^2r^2+32ebL\mathbb{E}\left\{Z_n(r)\right\}+8bLu}\Big)\le 2\exp\Big(-\frac{nu^2}{8eL^2r^2+128ebL^2\mathcal{R}_n(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F},r)+8bLu}\Big)$.
    
    Because $star\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}\right)$ is star-shaped, by the arguments in the proof of Lemma 13.6 of \cite{wainwright2019high}, the function $\delta\mapsto\frac{\mathcal{R}_n\left(star\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}\right),\delta\right)}{\delta}$ is non-decreasing on the interval $(0,\infty)$. Also, since $I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}\subset star\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}\right)$, then, for any $r\ge\delta_n$, it holds $\mathcal{R}_n\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F},r\right)/r\le\mathcal{R}_n\left(star\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}\right),r\right)/r\le\mathcal{R}_n\left(star\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}\right),\delta_n\right)/\delta_n\le\frac{\delta_n}{b}$. Then, $\text{P}\{Z_n(r)\ge \frac{4Lr\delta_n}{b}+u\}\le\text{P}\{Z_n(r)\ge 4L \mathcal{R}_n(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F},r)+u\}\le 2\exp\Big(-\frac{nu^2}{8eL^2r^2+128eL^2r\delta_n+8bLu}\Big)$.

Suppose the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lemma:lemma11foster} hold. Let $h_f$ and $Z_n(r) $ be defined as in Lemma \ref{lemma:lemma11foster} and let $\delta_n$ be any solution to $\mathcal{R}_n\left(star\left(I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot\mathcal{F}\right),\delta\right)\le\frac{\delta^2}{b}$. For fixed $\theta>1$ define the event $\mathcal{E}:=\{\exists f\in\mathcal{F}:\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\Vert_2\ge\delta_n\text{ and } \big\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nh_f(O_i) \big\vert\ge \frac{5\theta L\delta_n}{b}\left\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\right\Vert_2\}$. Also, set $c_1=\left\{8b^2(1+17e)\right\}^{-1}$. Then, $\text{P}(\mathcal{E})\le2\{ 1+I\{\delta_n<b/\theta\}\lfloor\{\log(\theta)\}^{-1}\log(b/\delta_n)\rfloor\} \:\exp(-c_1n\delta_n^2)$ where $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer smaller than or equal to $x$.
     \label{lemma:lemma12foster}

title: Proof
body_md:
This proof uses a peeling argument as in the proof of Lemma 12 of \citet*{foster2023orthogonal}. Since $\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\Vert_2\le \Vert f\Vert_{2}\le\Vert f\Vert_{\infty}$, Assumption 1.1 of Lemma \ref{lemma:lemma11foster} implies that $\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\Vert_{2}\le b$ for any $f\in\mathcal{F}$. Then, any $f\in\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\Vert_2\ge \delta_n$ belongs to the set $\mathcal{S}_m:=\{f\in\mathcal{F}\text{ }\::\:\text{ }\theta^{m-1}\delta_n\le\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\Vert_2\le \theta^m\delta_n\}$ for some $m\in\left\{1,\cdots,M\right\}$ where $M$ is the smallest integer satisfying $b\le \theta^M \delta_n$. We find such $M$ as follows. If $\delta_n\ge b/\theta$ then $M=1$ is such constant because $\theta>1$. If $\delta_n<b/\theta$ then $b\le \theta^M \delta_n$ iff $\log(b/\delta_n)\le M\log(\theta)$ iff $\left\{\log(\theta)\right\}^{-1}\log(b/\delta_n)\le M$. Therefore, we conclude that $M=1+I\{\delta_n<b/\theta\}\lfloor\{\log(\theta)\}^{-1}\log(b/\delta_n)\rfloor$. Note that $M$ is a positive integer because $\theta>1$ and $b/\delta_n>\theta$ when $\delta_n<b/\theta$.
    
    Now, if the event $\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{S}_m$ occurs for some $m\in\{1,\dots,M\}$, then there exists $f$ with $\theta^{m-1}\delta_n\le\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\Vert_2\le r_m:=\theta^m\delta_n$ such that $\vert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nh_f(O_i) \vert\ge \frac{5\theta L\delta_n}{b}\left\Vert I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f\right\Vert_2
    \ge \frac{5\theta L\delta_n}{b} \frac{r_m}{\theta} =5 \frac{L\delta_n r_m}{b}$.
    Consequently, we have $\text{P}\left(\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{S}_m\right)\le\text{P}\left[Z_n(r_m)\ge5 \frac{L\delta_n r_m}{b}\right]$. Applying Lemma \ref{lemma:lemma11foster} with $r=r_m$ and $u=\frac{L\delta_nr_m}{b}$, and setting $c_1=\left\{8b^2(1+17e)\right\}^{-1}$, we obtain that $\text{Pr}\left(\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{S}_m\right)$ happens with probability at most $2\exp\Big\{-\frac{nL^2r_m^2\delta_n^2}{8b^2(eL^2r_m^2+16eL^2\delta_nr_m+L^2\delta_nr_m)}\Big\}
    \le 2\exp\left(-c_1n\delta_n^2\right)$ where the inequality holds since $\delta_n\le r_m$. Then $\text{P}(\mathcal{E})\le\sum_{m=1}^M\text{P}(\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{S}_m)\le 2M\exp(-c_1 n\delta_n^2)=2\{ 1+I\{\delta_n<b/\theta\}\lfloor\{\log(\theta)\}^{-1}\log(b/\delta_n)\rfloor\}\exp\left(-c_1n\delta_n^2\right)$.

The proof proceeds similarly to that of Lemma~\ref{lemma:erm}, with minor changes to handle the terms  $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\{m(O;g)\}$ and $\mathbb{E}_n\{m(O;g)\}$. Here, $\xi(\delta_n)$ is as defined in~\ref{lemma:erm}, and the constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ are as in Lemma~\ref{lemma:erm}, except that $L'$ and $b$ are now $L' := \max\left\{1,\; \|r\|_\infty \cdot k_1 B,\; 2c^2 \cdot b \right\}$ and $ b:=B_1\max\{k_2,B_3\}$,
with $B_3$ being the constant specified in Assumption~\ref{ass:bounded}.

To use Lemma~\ref{lemma:lemma14foster} to bound $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\{m(O;g_{\tilde h})\}$, define $\mathcal{F}:=\{f(\cdot) :=m(\cdot;g):\mathcal{O}\mapsto\mathbb{R}\:|\: g\in\mathcal{G}_{B_1}\}$, $t_f:=f$, and $\mathcal{O}_0:=\mathcal{O}\text{ (equivalently $I_{\mathcal{O}_0}=1$)}$. We verify conditions (a)--(f) listed in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:erm}, which are required for Lemma~\ref{lemma:lemma14foster}. Condition (a) follows immediately from part 2 of Assumption~\ref{ass:bounded}.  Condition (a.3) holds because $g=0$ belongs to $\mathcal{G}_{B_1}$ and therefore $f_0:=0=m(\cdot,0)$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}$ by the linearity of $m$. Next, for any $f \in \mathcal{F}$, $f=m(\:\cdot\:,g_f)$ for some $g\in\mathcal{G}_{B_1}$. Then, 
    \begin{align*}
    |f(o)| = |f(o)-f_0(o)|\le B_3\cdot d(f,f_0)= B_3\cdot d(m(o;g_f),m(o,0))
    \le B_3\Vert g_f-0\Vert_\mathcal{G}\le B_3B_1,
    \end{align*} 
    where the first and second inequalities follow by part 2 of Assumption \ref{ass:bounded}, and the third holds because $g_f \in \mathcal{G}_{B_1}$. Thus, $\mathcal{F}$  is uniformly bounded by $B_3B_1\le b$, and so it satisfies condition (a.1). Condition (a.2) follows from part 2 of Assumption~\ref{ass:bounded}, which implies for all $o\in\mathcal{O}$ and $f_1,f_2\in\mathcal{F}$ that $ |f_1(o)-f_2(o)|\le\sup_{o\in\mathcal{O}}|f_1(o)-f_2(o)|\le B_3\cdot d(f_1,f_2)$. Condition (b) holds by the assumption on $m$ specified in Section \ref{sec:targer_param}. Condition (c) holds because $t_{I_{\mathcal{O}_0}\cdot f}=f$ and therefore (c) is the same as (a.2) that we have already argued to hold. Condition (d) holds because the last display implies $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\{|f_1(O)-f_2(O)|\}\le\sup_{o\in\mathcal{O}}|f_1(o)-f_2(o)|\le  B_3\cdot d(f_1,f_2)$. Condition (e) trivially holds because $t_f=f$. Likewise, (f) trivially holds with $L=1\le L'$.
